Fleming, Julie Fluhr, Christian Itty, Sergio Lambertucci, Kamran Safi, Emily Shepard, Justin M. Calabrese

## **Appendix S2**

## **Section 1: Considerations about the link function**

In statistics, link functions are routinely used to transform a bounded random variable of interest (e.g., a probability that varies between 0 and 1, or a count that is always positive) into a variable that varies between + and - ∞ . The effect of this transformation on the inference is rarely assessed, yet it is not always negligible (Pregibon 1980).

In our study of flight height, the ground constituted a hard boundary to vertical movement. Any observation of flight below the ground elevation was an obvious indication that either the flight height data, the ground elevation data, or both, were erroneous.

The intuitive solution is to use a truncated distribution (e.g., Brost _et al._ 2015), cutting at the expected altitude of the ground. However, 1) in order to use the Laplace approximation framework (Kristensen _et al._ 2014), all random variables need to be Gaussian distributed, which is incompatible with truncation; 2) the ground elevation itself is not known with precision.

Rather than using a truncated distribution, we worked with a Gaussian-distributed variable z’, which we back-transformed into an always positive variable z, representing the flight height above ground. The movement process applied to z’, but the observation process applied to z.

The standard link function to operate such a projection between R[+∗] and R is the log function, widely used in e.g., the generalized linear model framework. However, this function is strongly nonlinear. This would affect the estimation of temporal autocorrelation in the movement process. Indeed, velocities

dz′ = estimated on the log scale are very different to those estimated on the identity (natural) scale: dt dlog z 1 dz dt = z dt .

We thus looked for a link function that was linear for most of the flight range, but still diverged towards - ∞ when flight height approached the ground. In addition to that property, the function needed to be continuous with continuous first and second derivatives, monotonous (always positive first derivative), and easily invertible. ## **Section 2: Derivation of the collision risk model**

First, we assume that thermals are not a limiting resource: there is always a thermal within reach. Following Akos, Nagy & Vicsek (2008) and references therein, we approximate the flight trajectory as a succession of vertical ascensions in thermals (red lines in Fig. S1) followed by gliding bouts (green line in Fig. A1) during which the bird travels cross-country to the next thermal while losing elevation. This is an approximation because we neglect horizontal movement happening while in thermals (circles, drift) and assume that entry and exit heights depend on the uplift speed in the first thermal.

**Fig. S1** : Schematic representation of one iteration of the thermal soaring / inter-thermal gliding loop mentioned in the main text. In red, the bird gains altitude by using the uplift speed of thermals. In green, the bird glides cross countries and loses potential energy.

We denote h0 the entry height (the flight height at which the birds enter the thermal), _h_ the exit height ( h> h0 ), L the cross-country distance between the two thermals, _w_ the average vertical uplift speed while in thermal, _**v**_ the velocity during the gliding bout (with horizontal component vx and vertical component vz < 0 ). We define the risk zone as the flight height band that would be swept by turbine rotors if a turbine was erected. This risk zone is of height _a_ . Lastly, we consider that the bird is optimizing its exit height and its gliding velocity under a time constraint, and denote the optimal exit height h[∗] and the optimal gliding velocity v[∗] = (vx[∗] , vz[∗] ) .

Based on basic trigonometry, the time spent in the rotor-swept zone during one iteration of the thermal/inter-thermal glide sequence can be expressed as a function of _a_ , _w_ , and vz[∗] (Fig. S1). When D flying cross country over a distance _D_ , the bird in this model spends a time t = ∙(t1 + t2) where L t1 + t2 (defined in Fig. S1) denotes the time spent in the rotor-swept zone during one iteration of the thermal/inter-thermal glide sequence, and D/L is the number of iterations. There is also a simple trigonometric relationship between the cross-country distance L and _h_ * and _**v**_ * (Fig. S1). Replacing the 1 1 vz[∗] formula for t1 , t2 , and _L_ in the equation for _t_ , we get that t= D∙a∙ + ∙ . Further replacing ~~(~~ w vz[∗] ~~)~~ vx[∗] ∙h vz[∗] by the polar curve (cf. main text), _h_ * by its relationship with _w_ (cf. the main text), and vx[∗] by its relationship with _w_ (Eq. 1 in the main text), we obtain Eq. 2 in the main text.

Our final model (Eq. 3 in the main text) is based on the above elements, but we furthermore relax the constraint that thermals are not a limiting resource. In our final model, the bird can alternate between thermal and orographic uplifts based on the availability of the former and the cost/benefit balance of using thermal uplift instead of orographic uplift.

## **Section 3: Metrics for the amount of variance explained by a binomial**

## **nonlinear model**

MacFadden’s r[2] was computed as 1 −Dev/Dev0 where Dev is the model deviance and Dev0 is the n1 n0 deviance of the full model computed as n1log 0log with n0 and n1 the numbers ~~(~~ n0+n1) −n ~~(~~ n0+n1) of zeros and ones respectively. McFadden’s r[2] can be interpreted as a correlation coefficient, although it tends to underestimate the amount of variance explained. We also computed Somer's (1962) index

A−B of association, computed as D= where _N_ is the number of pairs of data points with different N−C values (zero or one), _A_ is the number of pairs where the model predictions agree with the observed values (i.e., a point recorded as zero is predicted to be lower risk than a point recorded as one), _B_ is the number of pairs where the model predictions disagree with the observed values (i.e., a point recorded as zero is predicted to be higher risk than a point recorded as one), and _C_ is the number of ties (i.e., a point recorded as zero is predicted to be at equal risk to a point recorded as one). Somer’s _D_ varies between -1 if the model predictions are always wrong to +1 if the model predictions are always correct.

## **Section 4: Supplemental figures**

**Fig. S2** : Left column: Relationship between estimated flight height, corrected for observation error using the state-space model, and orographic uplift potential. Compare to Fig. 2 in the main text. There is no relationship to orographic uplift potential. Right column: Relationship between estimated vertical velocity and orographic uplift potential. Vertical velocity is computed as the vertical displacement between to flight height records, corrected for observation error using the state-space model, and divided by the time interval between the records. Note the different scales for each species. Compare to Fig. 2 in the main text. There is no relationship to orographic potential.

**Fig. S3** : Semivariogram of the vulture flight data (b), after thinning them to mimic the sampling schedule of the condor data, plotted alongside the semivariogram for the condor data (a) to show that the sampling rate does not affect the fact that the autocorrelation time (the rate at which the semivariogram reaches its horizontal asymptote) is shorter in the vultures than in the condors. Finer sampling however makes the pattern easier to detect (cf. Fig. 1 in the main text). Very coarse sampling rate (in this case sampling intervals >30 minutes) would have prevented the detection of autocorrelation because they exceed the characteristic autocorrelation times of these movement processes.

**Fig. S4** : Relationship between flight height above ground and ground elevation above sea level (asl) in the three study species. The red lines are the output of generalized additive models. The histograms represent the ground elevation values sampled along the paths of the study individuals

**Fig. S5** : Raw proportion of flight time spent in the rotor-swept zone (60-180m) for the three study species, as a function of ground elevation and thermal uplift potential (0: no flight height record in the risk zone; 1: all flight height records in the risk zone; after correction for observation error), showing the lack of effect of ground elevation for condors and vultures, and the interaction between thermal uplift potential and ground elevation for eagles (rightmost panel). The white contours delimit cells with more than 20 data points.
